title: The oak and the reeds
hook: the oak breaks in the storm, and the reeds bend and live (Aesop)

segments.voice: Yesterday, omphax: the fox who couldn't reach the bunch, and decided it was sour anyway. Your line was not sour, just high. Did you catch yourself calling something sour? Day sixty-eight.

A storm is coming over a river valley. The sky goes green, the wind gets loud, and everything standing up has to decide what to do about it. On the bank there's a huge oak, the kind of tree people have picnics under, the kind that looks like it will outlast all of us. And down at the water's edge there's a patch of reeds, thin as pencils, the kind nobody notices. The smart money is on the oak. The people who told this story counted on that. Today's story is the oak and the reeds.
screen: `A STORM OVER THE RIVER.` → `THE GREAT OAK.` → `THE THIN REEDS.`

segments.voice: It's another of Aesop's fables, and it comes down in more than one version, with one reed or many. Here's one telling. A great wind tears through the valley. The oak stands firm, because that's what oaks do. The wind keeps pushing, and the oak keeps refusing, until with a crack its roots rip out of the bank and it falls into the river. The current carries it downstream, past the reeds, which are standing there, a little ruffled, and fine. The oak asks how they survived, when something so small should have been flattened. And the reeds answer, more or less: you fought the wind, and it broke you. We bowed our heads, and let it pass over us. Look at what that answer isn't. The reeds didn't stop being reeds. When the storm moved on, they stood straight again, rooted in the same mud. Bending isn't the same as being blown away. And the oak's strength was real, and admirable, and no use in this one storm, because it had only one move. Some old versions add a moral: those who yield to what they can't fight come through it. Another reading is quieter. A few things in life are worth standing against. Most of what blows through an ordinary day isn't. A plan changed at the last minute is wind. The way someone loads the dishwasher is wind. Bend, and come back up.
screen: `THE OAK FIGHTS, AND FALLS.` · `CARRIED PAST THE REEDS.` · `THE REEDS BOW, AND STAND AGAIN.` · `MOST OF A DAY'S WIND ISN'T WORTH IT.` · then, large: `BEND, DON'T BREAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bend on one small thing today. Settle, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one small thing you've been holding stiff about: a plan someone changed, a habit of someone you live with, a word that bugs you. Notice where you hold it in your body, maybe the jaw, maybe the shoulders. Now picture the reeds at the water's edge, bowing as the wind goes over. On each out-breath, let that place in your body bend a little. You're not giving up who you are. You're letting one gust pass. The bell holds the time.
reeds. Thin stems that bow, let the storm pass, and stand up again, while the strong oak that fought it breaks.

Your line: bend, don't break. Today, when some small thing doesn't go your way, try bowing your head to it the way the reeds did, and notice that you're still standing when it passes. Day sixty-eight.

howItsDone: People who read Aesop as everyday wisdom often reach for the oak and the reeds when they talk about flexibility: letting small things pass while keeping one's roots.

fork.setup: you're the reeds. the storm is here, and the wind is roaring. what do you do?
options: stand tall and fight it, like the oak
bow your heads and let it pass over
let go of the bank and float away
fork.reveal: they bow. the oak stands, is torn out, and floats downstream past them. afterward the reeds stand up again where they were.

original.note: Greek: reed. the fables come down to us in Greek, and this is the plant that bends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fable telling you to be a pushover.
what it means: bend to the storm you can't fight, then stand again, still rooted.
what a scholar hears: a fable of the Greek collections, retold in Latin by Avianus and later by La Fontaine.

notes: Fable paraphrased; confirm the Perry index number (70) and that versions in the Greek collections end with a moral about yielding.
Herodotus 2.134 names Aesop as a slave of Iadmon of Samos: confirm the reference.
Trapdoor: Avianus (fable 16) and La Fontaine (Fables I.22, Le Chene et le Roseau) retell it with one reed: confirm.
Greek κάλαμος (kalamos) for reed: confirm this is the word used in the Greek fable versions.
